prompt:
A swimmer of mass 68.0 kg dives into a deep diving pool. At the instant she is completely submerged, she is moving vertically downwards with a speed of 5.50 m s^-1. At this instant, the water exerts an upward buoyant force of 667 N and an upward viscous drag force of 380 N. The acceleration of free fall is 9.81 m s^-2.
[FIGURE PLACEHOLDER: Submerged swimmer moving vertically downwards, showing downward weight W, upward buoyant force B, and upward viscous drag D.]
(a) Calculate the weight of the swimmer. [1]
(b) Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant vertical force acting on the swimmer at this instant. [2]
(c) Calculate the swimmer's instantaneous acceleration. [1]
(d) Describe and explain how the viscous drag force and the acceleration of the swimmer change as her downward speed decreases. [2]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the weight of the swimmer.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant vertical force acting on the swimmer at this instant.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Describe and explain how the viscous drag force and the acceleration of the swimmer change as her downward speed decreases.

part_enrichment.guidance: Use W = mg with m = 68.0 kg and g = 9.81 m s^-2.
part_enrichment.common_pitfall: Dividing mass by g or omitting units.

marking_points.criterion: Sums upward forces (667 + 380 = 1047 N) and subtracts downward weight (1047 - 667.1 = 379.9 N).
Resultant force = 380 N (or 379.9 N) directed vertically upwards.

part_enrichment.guidance: Calculate net force vector sum and specify upward direction.
part_enrichment.common_pitfall: Omitting the direction or adding all forces in the same direction.

marking_points.criterion: Acceleration a = F_net / m = 379.9 / 68.0 = 5.59 m s^-2 directed vertically upwards.

part_enrichment.guidance: Divide resultant upward force by mass.
part_enrichment.common_pitfall: Dividing drag force alone by mass.

marking_points.criterion: Viscous drag force decreases as speed decreases.
Resultant upward force decreases, so the magnitude of upward acceleration (deceleration) decreases.

part_enrichment.guidance: Link decreasing speed to decreasing drag, and decreasing drag to decreasing net force and deceleration.
part_enrichment.common_pitfall: Assuming drag remains constant or claiming acceleration increases.

hints: In (b), compare total upward forces (buoyancy + drag) with downward weight.
In (d), recall how drag depends on speed, and how net force depends on drag.
solution:
(a) W = mg = 68.0 * 9.81 = 667 N.
(b) Total upward force = 667 + 380 = 1047 N. F_net = 1047 - 667.1 = 380 N vertically upwards.
(c) a = F_net / m = 379.9 / 68.0 = 5.59 m s^-2 vertically upwards.
(d) As speed decreases, viscous drag force decreases because drag in a fluid decreases with decreasing speed. This reduces the upward resultant force, causing the magnitude of the deceleration to decrease.
teacher_walkthrough: Part (b): Upward forces = Buoyancy (667 N) + Drag (380 N) = 1047 N. Net force = 1047 - 667.1 = 379.9 N = 380 N upwards. Award C1, A1.
Part (c): a = 379.9 / 68.0 = 5.59 m s^-2 upwards. Award A1.
Part (d): State that drag decreases as speed decreases (B1), and that the net decelerating force and acceleration therefore decrease (B1).
